text:
Philip Rubin is a prominent figure in computational and cognitive science, known for his pioneering work in speech synthesis, speech production, and perception. He earned a BA in psychology and linguistics from Brandeis University and a PhD in experimental psychology from the University of Connecticut under the supervision of Michael Turvey, Ignatius Mattingly, Philip Lieberman, and Alvin Liberman.
Rubin's research spans multiple disciplines, combining computational, engineering, linguistic, physiological, and psychological approaches to study embodied cognition, particularly the biological bases of speech and language. He is best known for his foundational contributions to articulatory synthesis, speech perception, and signal processing. Key developments include the design of the ASY and SWS systems, which model speech production and use sinewave synthesis to explore perceptual organization and spatiotemporal aspects of speech signals. He also developed the HADES signal processing system and the SPIEL programming language, a predecessor to MATLAB.
A core component of Rubin’s work is his theoretical contribution to a dynamical systems perspective on speech, emphasizing spatiotemporal coordination and embodied cognition. He introduced the concept of "gestures" as units of articulatory action, which underlie the production of speech. This approach, which combines articulatory phonology, task dynamics, and gesture-based modeling, has been applied in systems like TADA, which generates articulatory models of English utterances from text input.
Rubin has held significant leadership roles in science policy and administration. From 2000 to 2003, he served as Director of the Division of Behavioral and Cognitive Sciences at the National Science Foundation (NSF), where he helped launch key programs including Cognitive Neuroscience, Human Origins, and Documenting Endangered Languages. He later returned to the NSF as a senior advisor in the Directorate for Social, Behavioral and Economic Sciences during the Obama administration.
He has also served in various science policy and advocacy roles, including Chair of the National Academies Board on Behavioral, Cognitive, and Sensory Sciences, and as the former Chairman of the Board of the Discovery Museum and Planetarium in Bridgeport, Connecticut. He is currently the President and Chair of the Board of Directors of the Federation of Associations in Behavioral and Brain Sciences (FABBS).
Rubin is deeply engaged in ethical issues related to emerging technologies, particularly in the areas of human subjects research and intelligence and security applications. He has served on the National Human Research Protection Advisory Committee and the Secretary's Advisory Committee on Human Research Protections. He has been a vocal critic of technologies like voice stress analysis, arguing that they are ineffective and based on false hypotheses. He also participated in the development of the National Research Council's Committee on Field Evaluation of Behavioral and Cognitive Sciences-Based Methods and Tools for Intelligence and Counter-Intelligence.
In addition to his scientific and policy work, Rubin has been involved in science communication and public engagement. He is a member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, the American Psychological Association, and the American Association for the Advancement of Science. He has received numerous awards, including Fellowships from the Acoustical Society of America, the American Association for the Advancement of Science, and the American Psychological Association, as well as the IEEE Senior Member and the National Academy of Public Administration.
Rubin is also active in the broader scientific community, serving on boards of institutions such as Haskins Laboratories and the University of Connecticut. He has been a key figure in promoting science and technology education, and his work continues to influence research in cognitive science, neuroscience, and human-computer interaction.
